easy.heading: Warming Up With Today's Morning Pips
easy.body:
Starting the day with the easy puzzle felt like a nice, gentle stretch for the brain. The first thing that caught my eye was that long equals region across the top row. Knowing that cells (0,0) through (0,3) all had to be the same number really narrowed things down. Since almost all the dominoes available had a 0 in them, it was a safe bet that the top row was going to be a string of zeros. Once I placed that, the rest of the board started to fall into place like, well, dominoes!

The real breakthrough was the sum constraint in the corner. I needed (1,3) and (2,3) to add up to 10. Looking at my remaining tiles, the only way to make that happen without a double-five was to use the [1,5] and [0,5] dominoes. By putting (2,3) as 5 and (1,3) as 5, I hit that 10 perfectly. From there, I just had to check the greater than and less than signs. Putting the [6,0] domino at (1,1) satisfied the greater than 4 rule, and the [2,0] tile fit perfectly in the less than 4 spot. It was a super satisfying solve to finish over my first cup of coffee.

medium.heading: Stepping Up the Logic with Rodolfo
medium.body:
Rodolfo Kurchan really knows how to make a medium puzzle feel like a proper mystery. I spent a good few minutes staring at that tiny sum of 2 for the three cells in the upper right. Since we are dealing with domino pips, having three cells add up to only 2 is very restrictive. I realized quickly that the only way to make it work was to use the [1,1] domino for cells (1,4) and (1,5), which left (2,4) needing to be a 0. That forced the [0,6] domino into that area, helping me clear out the top right of the board.

Down at the bottom, the sum of 10 for (5,1) and (5,2) was the next big challenge. With the [5,5] domino in the list, it was the obvious candidate, but I had to be careful about which cell it actually occupied. I eventually saw that by pairing the [5,2] domino with the [5,5] tile, I could satisfy both the sum of 10 and the sum of 3 near the bottom left. The logic felt a bit like a dance, moving back and forth between the sums until every piece clicked into its home.

hard.heading: A True Tuesday Brain Workout
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today was a real journey! I actually got stuck for a second right in the middle. The huge sum of 12 across cells (5,4), (5,5), and (5,6) was the anchor for the whole grid. To get a sum that high, I knew I needed to use some of the biggest pips available, like the [4,5] and [3,6] dominoes. Once I committed to those being the core of that region, the rest of the bottom half started to make sense. I particularly liked how the sum of 7 at (9,5) and (9,6) played off the greater than 0 constraint nearby—it felt like a clever little trap if you weren't paying attention.

The hardest part for me was the top left corner. Balancing the sum of 7 with the greater than 4 requirement at (0,0) took some trial and error. I initially tried to put the [5,2] domino there, but it messed up the sum of 5 in the middle of the board. The breakthrough moment came when I realized the [1,6] domino had to live near the top to satisfy that 7 sum. After that, the remaining tiles like [0,2] and [2,4] fit into their spots like they were meant to be there all along. Finishing this one felt like a real victory!

explanation.tips: Always look for the smallest or largest sums first, as they have the fewest possible combinations. If you see a greater than or less than sign, use it to eliminate high or low numbers from your options immediately. Don't be afraid to pencil in a domino and see if it breaks a rule later—sometimes seeing what doesn't work is the fastest way to find what does!
explanation.learned: Today really highlighted how much a single 'equals' or 'sum' region can dictate the flow of the entire puzzle. In the easy grid, that row of zeros was like a skeleton that everything else hung onto. I also noticed that in harder puzzles, the constraints are often placed just far enough apart that you have to visualize how two different dominoes will interact before you can place either one.

faqs.question: What are the rules for NYT Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: In Pips, you place dominoes onto a grid so that every cell is covered. Each cell must follow the rules of its colored region, such as summing to a specific total, being equal to other cells, or satisfying greater than/less than conditions.

faqs.question: How do you solve the sum constraints in Pips?
faqs.answer: Look at the number of cells in the sum region and the target total. A small total like 2 for three cells almost always requires zeros and ones, while a large total like 12 requires high-value pips like 5s and 6s.

faqs.question: What does the 'empty' region type mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An 'empty' region simply means there is no additional numerical constraint on that specific cell. However, that cell must still be part of a valid domino and cannot violate the constraints of its domino partner.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes must always be placed either horizontally or vertically, covering two adjacent cells in the grid.

faqs.question: Are all dominoes in the list used in every Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Yes, every domino provided in the daily list must be used exactly once to completely fill the grid and satisfy all the region constraints.
